chapters.title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: After some resistance, Marianne gave in to her sister's pleas and agreed to go out with her and Mrs. Jennings for half an hour one morning. She made it an express condition, however, that they should pay no visits. She would only accompany them to Gray's in Sackville Street, where Elinor was arranging to exchange some old-fashioned jewellery belonging to their mother.

When they stopped outside, Mrs. Jennings remembered a lady at the other end of the street whom she ought to visit. Having no business of her own at Gray's, she agreed to make her call while her young friends dealt with theirs, and return to collect them afterwards.

Upstairs, the Miss Dashwoods found the room so crowded that nobody was free to attend to them, and they had to wait. They could do no more than sit at the end of the counter where they seemed most likely to be served soonest. Only one gentleman stood there, and Elinor probably hoped that politeness might persuade him to finish more quickly. But his exacting eye and refined taste proved stronger than his courtesy. He was ordering a toothpick case for himself. Until its size, shape, and decoration were settled—matters which he finally decided according to his own inventive fancy, after spending a quarter of an hour examining and discussing every toothpick case in the shop—he had no attention to spare for the ladies beyond three or four thoroughly unrestrained stares. These served to fix in Elinor's memory a face and figure distinguished by a strong, natural, solid insignificance, though dressed at the very height of fashion.

Marianne was spared the irritation and contempt which his rude inspection of their faces might have caused, as well as his affected deliberations over the various horrors of every toothpick case offered to him. She noticed none of it. In Mr. Gray's shop she could withdraw into her own thoughts and remain as unaware of everything around her as she could in her own bedroom.

At last the matter was settled. Ivory, gold, and pearls each received their appointed place. Having specified the final day on which life would remain possible without his toothpick case, the gentleman drew on his gloves with leisurely care. He gave the Miss Dashwoods another glance, one that seemed to demand admiration rather than express it, and walked away with an air happily combining real self-satisfaction and pretended indifference.

Elinor immediately began her business and was just about to finish it when another gentleman appeared beside her. She looked up at his face and discovered, with some surprise, that it was her brother.

Their affection and pleasure at meeting were sufficient to make a very respectable impression in Mr. Gray's shop. John Dashwood was genuinely far from sorry to see his sisters again; he was rather pleased. His questions about their mother were respectful and attentive.
Elinor learnt that he and Fanny had arrived in London two days earlier.

“I very much wanted to call on you yesterday,” he said, “but it was impossible. We had to take Harry to see the wild animals at Exeter Exchange, and spent the rest of the day with Mrs. Ferrars. Harry was tremendously pleased. _This_ morning I fully intended to visit you if I could possibly find half an hour free, but there is always so much to do when one first reaches London. I have come here to order a seal for Fanny. Tomorrow, though, I think I can certainly call in Berkeley Street and be introduced to your friend Mrs. Jennings. I understand she is very wealthy. And you must introduce me to the Middletons too. As relations of my stepmother, they may be sure I shall be glad to show them every respect. I hear they are excellent neighbours to you in the country.”
“Excellent indeed. I cannot adequately describe their concern for our comfort and their kindness in every possible way.”

“I am extremely glad to hear it, upon my word; extremely glad. But that is how it ought to be. They have large fortunes, they are related to you, and it is reasonable to expect every kindness and convenience that could make your circumstances pleasant. So you are comfortably settled in your little cottage, with nothing lacking! Edward gave us a most delightful account of it. The most perfect place of its kind, he said, and you all seemed to enjoy it beyond anything. I assure you, hearing that gave us great satisfaction.”
Elinor felt more than a little ashamed of her brother. She was glad to be spared an answer by the arrival of Mrs. Jennings's servant, who informed them that his mistress was waiting outside.
Mr. Dashwood accompanied them downstairs and was introduced to Mrs. Jennings at the carriage door. He repeated his hope of being able to visit the next day, then took his leave.

He duly paid his visit, bringing something that pretended to be an apology from his wife for not accompanying him: “She was so occupied with her mother that she really had no time to go anywhere.” Mrs. Jennings immediately assured him that she would not stand on ceremony. They were all cousins, or something like it, and she would certainly visit Mrs. John Dashwood very soon and bring his sisters with her. His manner towards _them_ was quiet but perfectly kind; towards Mrs. Jennings, attentively polite. When Colonel Brandon came in soon after him, he examined him with a curiosity which seemed to suggest that he needed only confirmation of his wealth to be equally polite to _him_.

After half an hour, he asked Elinor to walk with him to Conduit Street and introduce him to Sir John and Lady Middleton. The weather was unusually fine, and she readily agreed. His questions began as soon as they left the house.
“Who is Colonel Brandon? Does he have a fortune?”
“Yes. He owns a very good estate in Dorsetshire.”
“I am glad to hear it. He seems a thorough gentleman. And I think, Elinor, I may congratulate you on the prospect of a very respectable position in life.”
“Congratulate me, brother? What do you mean?”
“He is fond of you. I watched him closely and am certain of it. How large is his income?”
“About two thousand a year, I believe.”
“Two thousand a year.” Then, raising himself to a pitch of enthusiastic generosity, he added, “Elinor, for your sake I wish with all my heart it were _twice_ as much.”
“I do believe you,” Elinor answered. “But I am quite certain Colonel Brandon has not the slightest desire to marry _me_.”

“You are mistaken, Elinor, very much mistaken. A very small effort on your part will secure him. Perhaps he is undecided just now. Your small fortune may make him hesitate; all his friends may advise against it. But a few of those little attentions and encouragements which ladies find so easy will settle him, in spite of himself. There can be no reason why you should not try for him. One cannot suppose any previous attachment of yours—in short, you know an attachment of _that_ kind is quite out of the question. The objections cannot be overcome. You have too much sense not to understand that. Colonel Brandon must be the man. I shall spare no courtesy to make him pleased with you and your family. Everyone must be satisfied with such a marriage. In short, it is the sort of thing that”—he lowered his voice to an important whisper—“will be extremely welcome to _all concerned_.” Recollecting himself, he added, “That is, I mean, all your friends are truly anxious to see you well settled. Fanny especially: I assure you she has your interests very much at heart. Her mother too, Mrs. Ferrars, is a very kind woman. I am sure it would give her great pleasure; she said so herself the other day.”
Elinor did not consider this worthy of an answer.
“It would be remarkable,” he continued, “quite amusing, if Fanny's brother and my sister were to settle at the same time. And yet it is not at all unlikely.”
“Is Mr. Edward Ferrars going to be married?” Elinor asked with determination.

“Nothing is finally arranged, but something of that kind is under discussion. He has an excellent mother. If the marriage takes place, Mrs. Ferrars will act with the greatest generosity and settle a thousand a year on him. The lady is the Honourable Miss Morton, the late Lord Morton's only daughter, with thirty thousand pounds. A very desirable connection on both sides, and I have no doubt it will happen in time. A thousand a year is a great deal for a mother to give away permanently, but Mrs. Ferrars has a noble spirit. Here is another example of her generosity. The other day, just after we arrived in London, she knew we might not have much money available just now, and put two hundred pounds in banknotes into Fanny's hands. It is extremely welcome, since living here will cost us a great deal.”
He paused, waiting for agreement and sympathy. Elinor forced herself to reply.
“Your expenses in London and in the country must certainly be considerable. But you have a large income.”

“Not as large as many people imagine, I expect. Still, I do not mean to complain. It is certainly a comfortable income, and I hope it will improve in time. Enclosing Norland Common, which is going on now, is a very serious expense. Then I have made a little purchase in the past six months: East Kingham Farm. You must remember it, where old Gibson lived. In every respect the land was so desirable for me, lying directly beside my own property, that I felt it my duty to buy it. My conscience could not have allowed it to fall into other hands. A man must pay for convenience, and it _has_ cost me a great deal of money.”
“More than you think the land is actually worth in itself?”

“Well, I hope not. I could have sold it again the next day for more than I paid. But finding the purchase money might have been very unfortunate indeed. Stocks were so low then that, if I had not happened to have the necessary sum with my banker, I should have had to sell investments at a very heavy loss.”
Elinor could do nothing but smile.

“We had other large, unavoidable expenses on first moving to Norland, too. As you know, our respected father left your mother all the furnishings from Stanhill that remained at Norland, and they were very valuable. I would never complain of that. He had every right to dispose of his own property as he pleased. But the consequence was that we had to buy a great deal of linen, china, and so on to replace what was taken away. After all these expenses, you can imagine how far we must be from wealthy, and how welcome Mrs. Ferrars's kindness is.”
“Certainly,” Elinor said. “With the help of her generosity, I hope you may yet live to find yourselves comfortably off.”

“Another year or two may do a great deal,” he answered gravely. “Still, much remains to be done. Not one stone has been laid for Fanny's greenhouse, and the flower garden has gone no further than having its plan marked out.”
“Where do you intend to put the greenhouse?”

“On the little hill behind the house. All the old walnut trees have been cut down to make room. It will look very fine from many parts of the park, and the flower garden will slope down in front of it and be exceedingly pretty. We have cleared away all the old thorn bushes that grew in patches along the brow.”
Elinor kept her distress and disapproval to herself, and was very grateful that Marianne was not there to feel the same provocation.

He had now said enough to establish his poverty and free himself from any obligation to buy each sister a pair of earrings on his next visit to Gray's. His thoughts took a happier turn, and he began congratulating Elinor on having a friend like Mrs. Jennings.

“She certainly seems a most valuable woman. Her house and her way of living both indicate an extremely good income. This is an acquaintance that has already been very useful to you, and may eventually bring substantial advantages. Her invitation to London is certainly much in your favour. Indeed, everything shows such affection for you that she will probably remember you when she dies. She must have a great deal to leave.”
“I should rather think she has nothing at all. She has only her widow's settlement, which will pass to her children.”
“But surely she does not spend her entire income. Few reasonably prudent people do _that_. And whatever she saves, she will be free to leave as she chooses.”
“Don't you think she is more likely to leave those savings to her daughters than to us?”

“Her daughters have both married extremely well, so I see no need for her to provide them with anything more. In my opinion, by paying you such attention and treating you so kindly, she has given you a sort of claim on her future consideration which a conscientious woman would not ignore. Nothing could be kinder than her behaviour. She can hardly do all this without realising the expectations it creates.”
“But it creates no such expectations in us. Really, brother, your concern for our welfare and prosperity is carrying you too far.”

“Well, certainly,” he said, appearing to recollect himself, “people can do little, very little, to help. But, my dear Elinor, what is wrong with Marianne? She looks very unwell, so pale and thin. Is she ill?”
“She is not well. She has been suffering from a nervous illness for several weeks.”

“I am sorry to hear it. At her age, any illness destroys a girl's bloom for ever! Hers has lasted such a short time. Last September she was as handsome a girl as I ever saw, and as likely to attract a man. Her particular kind of beauty had something men especially like. I remember Fanny saying she would marry sooner and better than you. Not that she is not exceedingly fond of _you_; it simply struck her that way. But she will be proved wrong. I doubt whether Marianne _now_ will marry anyone with more than five or six hundred a year at most, and I shall be much mistaken if _you_ do not do better. Dorsetshire! I know very little of Dorsetshire, but, my dear Elinor, I should be delighted to learn more. I think I can promise that Fanny and I will be among your earliest and happiest visitors.”

Elinor tried very earnestly to convince him that she was not likely to marry Colonel Brandon. But the expectation gave him too much pleasure to surrender. He was genuinely determined to become the gentleman's close acquaintance and encourage the marriage by every possible attention. He felt just enough guilt about having done nothing for his sisters himself to be extremely anxious that everyone else should do a great deal. A proposal from Colonel Brandon or an inheritance from Mrs. Jennings would be the easiest way to make up for his own neglect.

They were fortunate enough to find Lady Middleton at home, and Sir John returned before their visit ended. Polite attentions were exchanged abundantly on every side. Sir John was willing to like anyone. Although Mr. Dashwood seemed to know little about horses, he soon decided he was a very good-natured fellow. Lady Middleton found his appearance fashionable enough to make his acquaintance worth having. Mr. Dashwood left delighted with them both.

“I shall have a delightful account to give Fanny,” he said as he walked back with his sister. “Lady Middleton is really a most elegant woman! Exactly the sort of person Fanny will be pleased to know. And Mrs. Jennings too is exceedingly well-mannered, though less elegant than her daughter. Your sister-in-law need have no hesitation about visiting even _her_. To tell the truth, she has had some doubts, and very naturally. All we knew was that Mrs. Jennings was the widow of a man who had made his money in a low kind of business. Fanny and Mrs. Ferrars were both firmly persuaded that neither she nor her daughters would be women Fanny wished to associate with. But now I can give her a thoroughly satisfactory account of them both.”

chapters.title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: Mrs. John Dashwood trusted her husband's judgement so completely that the very next day she visited both Mrs. Jennings and her daughter. Her trust was rewarded. Even Mrs. Jennings, even the woman with whom her sisters-in-law were staying, proved by no means unworthy of her attention. As for Lady Middleton, she found her one of the most delightful women in the world.

Lady Middleton was equally pleased with Mrs. Dashwood. A certain cold-hearted selfishness in each drew them together. They understood one another perfectly in the dull correctness of their behaviour and their general lack of intelligence.

The manners that won Lady Middleton's approval, however, did not appeal to Mrs. Jennings. To _her_, Mrs. John Dashwood appeared merely a small, proud-looking woman with an unfriendly manner, who met her husband's sisters without affection and almost without anything to say. Of the fifteen minutes she granted Berkeley Street, she spent at least seven and a half in silence.

Elinor very much wanted to know whether Edward was in London, though she chose not to ask. But nothing could have persuaded Fanny to mention his name voluntarily in front of her until she could announce his marriage to Miss Morton as settled, or until her husband's hopes concerning Colonel Brandon had been fulfilled. She believed Edward and Elinor still so attached that no effort to separate them, in conversation and in practice, could be too thorough. The information _she_ withheld soon came from elsewhere. Lucy arrived shortly afterwards to claim Elinor's sympathy because she could not see Edward, although he had come to London with Mr. and Mrs. Dashwood. He dared not visit Bartlett's Buildings for fear of discovery. Though their impatience to meet was, she said, beyond description, they could do nothing for the present except write.

Before long, Edward himself confirmed his presence in London by calling twice in Berkeley Street. Twice they returned from their morning engagements to find his card on the table. Elinor was pleased that he had called, and still more pleased to have missed him.

The Dashwoods were so extraordinarily delighted with the Middletons that, although not accustomed to giving much of anything, they decided to give them a dinner. Soon after the acquaintance began, they invited them to Harley Street, where they had rented a very good house for three months. The sisters and Mrs. Jennings were invited too. John Dashwood took care to secure Colonel Brandon, who was always glad to be wherever the Miss Dashwoods were. He received John's eager politeness with some surprise, but considerably more pleasure. Mrs. Ferrars would be there, though Elinor could not discover whether either of her sons was also invited. The prospect of meeting _her_ was enough to make Elinor interested in the evening. She could now meet Edward's mother without the intense anxiety she had once expected such an introduction to cause. She could be completely indifferent to the woman's opinion of her. Yet her wish to meet Mrs. Ferrars, and her curiosity about what she was like, remained as strong as ever.
Soon afterwards, she learnt that the Miss Steeles would be there as well. This increased her interest in the dinner more powerfully than pleasantly.

Their persistent attentions had made them so agreeable to Lady Middleton, and won her approval so thoroughly, that she was as willing as Sir John to invite them to Conduit Street for a week or two. Lucy was certainly not elegant, and her sister not even well-mannered, but that made no difference. Once the Dashwoods' invitation became known, it happened to be particularly convenient for the Miss Steeles to begin their stay a few days before the dinner.

Being the nieces of the gentleman who had educated her brother for so many years might not, by itself, have secured them seats at Mrs. John Dashwood's table. As Lady Middleton's guests, however, they had to be welcome. Lucy had long wished to know the family personally, to examine their characters and her own difficulties at closer range, and to have an opportunity to please them. She had seldom felt happier than when Mrs. John Dashwood's invitation arrived.

It had a very different effect on Elinor. She immediately persuaded herself that Edward, who was staying with his mother, must be invited along with her to a dinner at his sister's house. To see him for the first time after everything that had happened, and in Lucy's company—she scarcely knew how she could endure it.

These fears were perhaps not entirely reasonable, and were certainly not at all accurate. They were relieved, however, by no reconsideration of Elinor's own, but by Lucy's kindness. Lucy believed she was inflicting a severe disappointment when she announced that Edward would certainly not be in Harley Street on Tuesday. She even hoped to deepen the pain by persuading Elinor that he stayed away because his love for Lucy was too great to conceal when they were together.
The important Tuesday arrived, when the two young women were to be introduced to this formidable prospective mother-in-law.

“Pity me, dear Miss Dashwood!” Lucy said as they went upstairs together. The Middletons had arrived so close behind Mrs. Jennings that they all followed the servant at once. “There is nobody here except you who can understand what I feel. I declare I can hardly stand. Good heavens! In a moment I shall see the person on whom all my happiness depends—the woman who is to be my mother!”

Elinor could have relieved her immediately by suggesting that they might be about to meet Miss Morton's future mother-in-law rather than her own. Instead, she assured Lucy with complete sincerity that she did pity her. This utterly astonished Lucy, who, though genuinely uncomfortable herself, had hoped at least to inspire uncontrollable envy in Elinor.

Mrs. Ferrars was a small, thin woman, so upright that her posture seemed ceremonial, and so serious that her expression was sour. Her skin was sallow and her features small, neither beautiful nor naturally expressive. A fortunate tightening of her brow had saved her face from the disgrace of blankness by giving it unmistakable signs of pride and bad temper. She said little, for unlike most people she kept the number of her words proportionate to the number of her ideas. Of the few syllables she did utter, not one was directed towards Elinor, whom she examined with a vigorous determination to dislike her whatever happened.

Such behaviour could not make Elinor unhappy _now_. A few months earlier it would have hurt her deeply; now Mrs. Ferrars had no power to distress her in that way. The contrast in her treatment of the Miss Steeles, seemingly designed to humiliate Elinor still further, only amused her. She could not help smiling at the graciousness of both mother and daughter towards the very person—Lucy was singled out especially—whom they would most have wished to mortify if they had known what Elinor knew. Meanwhile Elinor herself, comparatively powerless to hurt them, was pointedly ignored by both. Yet, while she smiled at kindness so wrongly directed, she could not consider the petty foolishness behind it, or observe the calculated attentions with which the Miss Steeles encouraged it, without feeling complete contempt for all four women.
Lucy was triumphant at being so flatteringly singled out. Miss Steele needed only to be teased about Dr. Davies to make her happiness complete.

The dinner was magnificent, the servants numerous, and everything declared the mistress's love of display and the master's ability to pay for it. Despite the improvements and additions at Norland, and despite its owner's having once come within several thousand pounds of being obliged to sell investments at a loss, nothing suggested the poverty he had tried to imply. No shortage of any kind appeared, except a shortage of conversation—and that was considerable. John Dashwood had little to say worth hearing, and his wife had even less. But this was no particular disgrace among such company. Most of their guests suffered from one or another of the same obstacles to being agreeable: a lack of intelligence, whether natural or cultivated; a lack of elegance; a lack of spirits; or a lack of good temper.

This poverty became especially clear when the ladies withdrew to the drawing room after dinner. The gentlemen _had_ provided some variety of conversation: politics, the enclosure of land, and training horses. But that was now over. Until coffee arrived, the ladies discussed just one subject: whether Harry Dashwood or Lady Middleton's second son, William, was the taller, the two boys being nearly the same age.

Had both children been present, the matter might have been settled too easily by measuring them. But only Harry was there, leaving both sides free to make confident guesses. Everyone had an equal right to certainty, and to repeat their opinion as often as they wished.
The positions were these:
Each mother, privately certain her own boy was taller, politely gave the advantage to the other's son.
The two grandmothers were just as partial but more honest, each earnestly defending the claims of her own grandson.

Lucy was almost equally anxious to please both mothers. She thought both boys remarkably tall for their age and could not imagine the slightest difference between them. Miss Steele, with still greater tact, gave her opinion in favour of each in turn as rapidly as possible.

Having once stated that she thought William taller, and thereby offended Mrs. Ferrars and Fanny still further, Elinor saw no need to reinforce her opinion by repeating it. When Marianne was asked for hers, she offended everyone by declaring that she had none, since she had never thought about the matter.

Before leaving Norland, Elinor had painted a very pretty pair of decorative screens for Fanny. Newly mounted and delivered, they now ornamented her drawing room. John Dashwood noticed them as he followed the other gentlemen into the room, and busily placed them in Colonel Brandon's hands for him to admire.

“My eldest sister painted these,” he said. “As a man of taste, I dare say you will enjoy them. I don't know whether you have seen any of her work before, but she is generally considered to draw extremely well.”

The Colonel denied any claim to expert judgement, but warmly admired the screens, as he would have admired anything Elinor had painted. Naturally, the others became curious, and the screens were passed round for inspection. Mrs. Ferrars, unaware who had painted them, specifically asked to see them. After they had received the gratifying evidence of Lady Middleton's approval, Fanny handed them to her mother, considerately explaining at the same moment that they were Miss Dashwood's work.
“Hmm,” said Mrs. Ferrars. “Very pretty.” Without looking at them at all, she handed them back to her daughter.
Perhaps Fanny thought for a moment that her mother had been quite rude enough. She coloured slightly and immediately said,
“They really are very pretty, aren't they, ma'am?” But then she was probably seized by the fear that she herself had been too polite, too encouraging, for she soon added,
“Don't you think they are rather in Miss Morton's style, ma'am? _She_ paints so delightfully! Her latest landscape is beautifully done, isn't it?”
“Beautifully indeed! But _she_ does everything to perfection.”

Marianne could not bear it. She was already deeply displeased with Mrs. Ferrars. Such ill-timed praise of someone else at Elinor's expense, though she did not understand its chief purpose, immediately provoked her into an indignant reply.
“What a peculiar sort of admiration! What is Miss Morton to us? Who knows anything about her, or cares? _We_ are thinking and speaking of Elinor.”
As she spoke, she took the screens from her sister-in-law's hands so that she could admire them herself as they deserved.
Mrs. Ferrars looked extremely angry. Drawing herself up more stiffly than ever, she delivered this scathing reply: “Miss Morton is the daughter of Lord Morton.”

Fanny looked very angry too, while her husband was thoroughly alarmed by his sister's boldness. Marianne's vehemence hurt Elinor much more than the conduct that had caused it. But Colonel Brandon's eyes, fixed on Marianne, showed that he saw only its lovable side: the affectionate heart that could not bear the smallest slight to a sister.

Marianne's feelings went further. Mrs. Ferrars's cold insolence towards Elinor seemed to predict troubles and unhappiness which her own wounded heart taught her to contemplate with horror. Moved by a powerful impulse of tender affection, she went after a moment to her sister's chair. Putting an arm round her neck and pressing her cheek close to hers, she spoke in a low but urgent voice.
“Dear, dearest Elinor, pay no attention to them. Don't let them make _you_ unhappy.”

She could say no more. Completely overcome, she hid her face on Elinor's shoulder and burst into tears. Everyone noticed; almost everyone felt concern. Colonel Brandon rose and came towards them without knowing what he was doing. With a very knowing “Ah, poor dear,” Mrs. Jennings immediately offered her smelling salts. Sir John was so furiously angry with the man responsible for this nervous distress that he at once moved beside Lucy Steele and whispered a brief account of the whole dreadful affair.
After a few minutes, however, Marianne recovered enough to end the commotion and sit among the others. The impression of what had happened remained with her spirits for the rest of the evening.

“Poor Marianne!” her brother said quietly to Colonel Brandon as soon as he could gain his attention. “She has not her sister's good health. She is very nervous; she lacks Elinor's constitution. And one must admit that losing her looks is very trying for a young woman who _has been_ a beauty. You might not think it, but a few months ago Marianne _was_ remarkably handsome, quite as handsome as Elinor. Now, you see, it is all gone.”

chapters.title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: Elinor's curiosity about Mrs. Ferrars was satisfied. She had found everything in her that could make any closer connection between their families undesirable. She had seen enough pride, pettiness, and determined prejudice against herself to understand all the difficulties that would have complicated her engagement to Edward and delayed their marriage, had he otherwise been free. She had almost seen enough to be grateful, for her _own_ sake, that one greater obstacle protected her from every obstacle Mrs. Ferrars might create: from dependence on her whims, and from any anxiety about her approval. Or, if Elinor could not quite rejoice that Edward was bound to Lucy, she at least decided that, had Lucy been more lovable, she _ought_ to have rejoiced.

She wondered how Lucy could be so elated by Mrs. Ferrars's politeness. Self-interest and vanity must blind her completely if attention seemingly paid only because she was _not Elinor_ appeared a compliment to herself, or if she could draw encouragement from a preference that depended on ignorance of her real position. Yet Lucy's eyes had clearly declared this at the time, and she made it still more explicit the next morning. At her particular request, Lady Middleton dropped her in Berkeley Street, in the hope of finding Elinor alone so that she could tell her how happy she was.
The chance worked in her favour. Soon after she arrived, a message from Mrs. Palmer called Mrs. Jennings away.

“My dear friend!” Lucy exclaimed as soon as they were alone. “I have come to tell you about my happiness. Could anything be more flattering than Mrs. Ferrars's treatment of me yesterday? She was so wonderfully friendly! You know how I dreaded meeting her. But the very moment we were introduced, she behaved so pleasantly that it really seemed to say she had quite taken a liking to me. Didn't it? You saw everything. Weren't you struck by it too?”
“She was certainly very polite to you.”

“Polite! Did you see nothing beyond politeness? I saw a great deal more. Nobody else received such kindness! There was no pride, no haughtiness, and your sister-in-law was exactly the same—all sweetness and friendliness!”
Elinor wanted to change the subject. But Lucy kept insisting that she acknowledge how justified her happiness was, and Elinor had to continue.
“Certainly, if they had known about your engagement,” she said, “their treatment could not have been more flattering. But since they did not know—”

“I knew you would say that,” Lucy interrupted quickly. “But there was no reason at all for Mrs. Ferrars to seem to like me if she didn't. And her liking me is everything. You will not talk me out of my pleasure. I am sure everything will end well, and the difficulties will be nothing compared with what I used to imagine. Mrs. Ferrars is a delightful woman, and so is your sister-in-law. They are both delightful! I wonder why I never heard you say how agreeable Mrs. Dashwood was.”
Elinor had nothing to say to this, and made no attempt to answer.
“Are you unwell, Miss Dashwood? You seem low. You say nothing. Surely you cannot be well.”
“I have never been in better health.”

“I am delighted to hear it, though you really didn't look well. I should be so sorry for _you_ to be ill, when you have been my greatest comfort in the world! Heaven knows what I should have done without your friendship.”
Elinor attempted a polite reply, though she doubted how well she managed it. Lucy seemed satisfied, however, and immediately answered,

“I am perfectly certain of your affection for me. After Edward's love, it is my greatest comfort. Poor Edward! But now there is one good thing: we shall be able to meet, and quite often too. Lady Middleton is delighted with Mrs. Dashwood, so I expect we shall spend a great deal of time in Harley Street. Edward spends half his time with his sister. Besides, Lady Middleton and Mrs. Ferrars will now visit each other, and both Mrs. Ferrars and your sister-in-law kindly said more than once that they would always be pleased to see me. Such charming women! If you ever tell your sister-in-law what I think of her, I am sure you cannot praise her too highly.”
Elinor gave her no encouragement to expect that she _would_ pass the message on. Lucy went on talking.

“I am sure I would have noticed immediately if Mrs. Ferrars had disliked me. Suppose she had merely given me a formal curtsy without a word, then ignored me for the rest of the evening and never once looked pleasantly at me—you understand what I mean. If she had treated me in that forbidding way, I should have given up everything in despair. I could not have borne it. For I know that when she _does_ dislike someone, she dislikes them violently.”
Before Elinor could reply to this courteous triumph, the door was thrown open, the servant announced Mr. Ferrars, and Edward walked straight in.

It was a painfully awkward moment, and every face showed it. They all looked extremely foolish. Edward seemed as ready to walk out again as to come any further into the room. The very situation each had most wanted to avoid had overtaken them in its worst possible form. Not only were all three together, but there was nobody else to ease the meeting. The women recovered first. It was not Lucy's place to put herself forward, and they still had to preserve the appearance of secrecy. She could therefore express her tenderness only through her _looks_. After briefly greeting him, she said nothing more.

Elinor had more to do. For Edward's sake and her own, she was so anxious to do it well that, after a moment to collect herself, she forced herself to welcome him with an expression and manner almost relaxed, almost open. Another struggle, another effort, made them better still. Neither Lucy's presence nor the knowledge that she herself had been treated unfairly would prevent her from saying she was glad to see him and had regretted being out when he called before in Berkeley Street. She would not let Lucy's observant eyes frighten her out of showing him the consideration owed to a friend who was almost a relation, though she soon realised how closely those eyes were watching her.

Her manner reassured Edward enough for him to sit down. His embarrassment nevertheless remained far greater than either woman's, to a degree that their circumstances explained, though his sex might make it unusual. His heart lacked Lucy's indifference, and his conscience could not share Elinor's complete ease.

With a modest, composed expression, Lucy seemed determined to do nothing for anyone else's comfort. She would not speak. Almost every word _that was_ spoken came from Elinor, who had to volunteer the information about her mother's health, their arrival in London, and other matters that Edward ought to have asked about but never did.

Her efforts did not end there. Before long, she felt heroic enough to decide to leave them alone on the excuse of fetching Marianne. She actually carried it out, and in the most generous way: with extraordinary strength of mind, she spent several minutes lingering on the landing before going to her sister. Once she had done that, however, Edward's raptures had to end, for Marianne's joy brought her immediately to the drawing room. Her pleasure at seeing him was, like every feeling of hers, intense and intensely expressed. She greeted him with a hand that insisted on being taken, and a voice full of a sister's affection.
“Dear Edward!” she cried. “What a happy moment this is! It could almost make up for everything!”

Edward tried to respond as her kindness deserved, but with such witnesses he dared not express half of what he felt. They all sat again, and for a moment or two nobody spoke. Marianne looked from Edward to Elinor with the most eloquent tenderness, regretting only that Lucy's unwelcome presence restrained their joy in each other. Edward spoke first, noticing the change in Marianne's appearance and expressing his fear that London did not agree with her.

“Oh, don't concern yourself with me!” she answered earnestly, though tears filled her eyes as she spoke. “Don't think about _my_ health. You can see that Elinor is well. That must be enough for both of us.”
This remark did nothing to ease either Edward's or Elinor's feelings, or to win Lucy's goodwill. Lucy looked up at Marianne with an expression far from kindly.
“Do you like London?” Edward asked, ready to say anything that might lead to a different subject.
“Not at all. I expected a great deal of pleasure here and have found none. Seeing you, Edward, is the only comfort it has given me. And thank heaven, you are still the person you always were!”
She paused. Nobody said a word.

“Elinor,” she soon continued, “I think we must ask Edward to look after us on our journey back to Barton. We shall probably leave in a week or two, and I trust he will not be too unwilling to undertake the responsibility.”

Poor Edward muttered something which nobody understood, including himself. But Marianne saw his agitation and could readily explain it in whatever way pleased her best. She was entirely satisfied, and soon moved on to another subject.
“What a day we spent in Harley Street yesterday, Edward! So dull, so miserably dull! But I have a great deal to tell you about that which I cannot say now.”

With this admirable discretion she postponed telling him that she found their shared relations more disagreeable than ever, and his mother especially disgusting, until they could speak more privately.
“But why weren't you there, Edward? Why didn't you come to the dinner?”
“I had another engagement.”
“Another engagement! But what could that matter, when such friends would be there?”
“Perhaps, Miss Marianne,” Lucy said, eager for a little revenge, “you think young men need never honour their engagements if they don't feel like keeping them—small ones or great ones.”
Elinor was very angry, but Marianne seemed not to feel the sting at all. She answered calmly,

“Certainly not. To speak seriously, I am quite sure that only conscience kept Edward away from Harley Street. I believe he _has_ the most sensitive conscience in the world, the most scrupulous about fulfilling every promise, however small, and however much it may interfere with his own interests or pleasure. Of everyone I know, he is the most afraid of causing pain or disappointing hopes, and the least capable of selfishness. Edward, it is true, and I will say it. What, must you never hear yourself praised? Then you cannot be my friend. Anyone who accepts my love and respect must accept my speaking openly in their praise.”
The particular nature of this praise was unfortunately ill suited to the feelings of two-thirds of her audience. Far from cheering Edward, it prompted him very soon to rise and take his leave.
“Leaving already!” Marianne exclaimed. “My dear Edward, you really must not go so soon.”

Drawing him a little aside, she whispered her conviction that Lucy could not stay much longer. Even that encouragement failed: he insisted on leaving. Lucy, who would have outstayed him if his visit had lasted two hours, departed soon afterwards.
“What brings her here so often?” Marianne asked once Lucy had gone. “Couldn't she see that we wanted her to leave? How irritating it must have been for Edward!”
“Why should it be? We were all his friends, and he has known Lucy longer than any of us. It is only natural that he should like seeing her as well as us.”

Marianne looked steadily at her. “You know, Elinor, that I cannot bear this kind of talk. If you only want me to contradict you, as I must suppose you do, you should remember that I am the last person in the world to oblige. I will not lower myself to being tricked into giving assurances that are not really needed.”

She left the room. Elinor dared not follow to say more. Bound by her promise to keep Lucy's secret, she could give no explanation that would convince Marianne. Painful as the consequences of her continuing mistake might be, Elinor had to accept them. She could only hope that Edward would not often expose either of them to the distress of hearing Marianne's mistaken enthusiasm, or to any repetition of the other pain their recent meeting had caused. She had every reason to expect that he would not.

chapters.title: Chapter 36
paragraphs: A few days after this meeting, the newspapers informed the world that the wife of Thomas Palmer, Esq., had safely given birth to a son and heir. It was a deeply interesting and satisfying announcement, at least to all the close relations and friends who already knew.

This event, so important to Mrs. Jennings's happiness, temporarily changed the way she spent her time and, to the same extent, the arrangements of her young guests. Wanting to be with Charlotte as much as possible, she left every morning as soon as she was dressed and returned only late in the evening. At the Middletons' special request, the Miss Dashwoods spent each entire day in Conduit Street. For their own comfort they would much rather have stayed at Mrs. Jennings's house, at least through the morning. But that preference could not be urged against everyone's wishes. Their hours were therefore handed over to Lady Middleton and the Miss Steeles, who in reality valued their company very little, however eagerly they professed to seek it.

The Dashwoods had too much intelligence to suit Lady Middleton as companions. The Miss Steeles, meanwhile, looked on them jealously, as intruders on _their_ territory who shared the kindness they wanted to monopolise. Lady Middleton could not have behaved more politely to Elinor and Marianne, yet she did not actually like them at all. Since they flattered neither her nor her children, she could not think them good-natured. Since they liked reading, she suspected them of being satirical. Perhaps she did not know exactly what being satirical meant, but _that_ was irrelevant. It was a common accusation, and an easy one to make.

Their presence restrained both her and Lucy. It interfered with one woman's idleness and the other's industry. Lady Middleton felt ashamed of doing nothing in front of them. Lucy feared their contempt for the flattery she was usually so proud to invent and deliver. Miss Steele was the least disturbed of the three, and the Dashwoods could have reconciled her completely to their presence. If either had given her a full, detailed account of everything between Marianne and Mr. Willoughby, she would have considered herself amply repaid for losing the best seat by the fire after dinner when they arrived. But no such compensation was offered. Though she often expressed pity for Marianne to Elinor, and more than once remarked in Marianne's hearing on the unfaithfulness of young men, she achieved only a look of indifference from one sister or disgust from the other. An even smaller effort might have won her friendship: if only they had teased her about the Doctor! But they were no more inclined to oblige than anyone else. When Sir John dined away from home, she might pass a whole day without hearing a single joke on the subject except those she kindly supplied herself.

Mrs. Jennings suspected none of these jealousies and grievances. She thought it delightful for the girls to spend time together, and usually congratulated her young friends each night on having escaped a tiresome old woman for so long. Sometimes she joined them at Sir John's, sometimes at her own house. Wherever they met, she arrived in excellent spirits, full of happiness and importance. She attributed Charlotte's good recovery to her own care, and was ready to give a report so precise and detailed that only Miss Steele had enough curiosity to welcome it. One thing _did_ trouble her, and she complained of it daily. Mr. Palmer held the opinion, common among men but unfatherly, that all babies looked alike. At different moments she could plainly see striking likenesses between this baby and every relation on both sides of the family. Yet nothing could persuade his father that he was not exactly like every other infant of the same age. He could not even be brought to acknowledge the simple fact that this was the finest child in the world.

I must now describe a misfortune that befell Mrs. John Dashwood about this time. During her sisters-in-law's first visit to Harley Street with Mrs. Jennings, another acquaintance had happened to call. In itself, that circumstance hardly seemed likely to harm her. But while other people's imaginations lead them into mistaken judgements of our behaviour, based on the slightest appearances, our happiness must always be partly at the mercy of chance. In this instance, the new arrival allowed imagination to run so far beyond truth and probability that, merely on hearing the Miss Dashwoods' name and learning that they were Mr. Dashwood's sisters, she immediately assumed they were staying in Harley Street. A day or two later, this mistake produced invitations for them, as well as their brother and his wife, to a small musical party at her house. Mrs. John Dashwood consequently had to endure not only the enormous inconvenience of sending her carriage for the sisters, but the still greater unpleasantness of appearing to pay them attention. And who could be sure they might not expect to accompany her a second time? Certainly, she would always have the power to disappoint them. But that was not enough. When people have resolved on conduct they know is wrong, they feel injured by any expectation that they might behave better.

By now Marianne had gradually become so accustomed to going out every day that she no longer cared whether she went or stayed. She prepared quietly and mechanically for each evening's engagement, expecting no pleasure from any of them, and often not knowing until the last moment where she was going.

She had become so indifferent to her clothes and appearance that, during the whole process of dressing, she gave them less than half the attention Miss Steele bestowed in the first five minutes after seeing her ready. Nothing escaped _that_ lady's close observation and general curiosity. She saw everything and asked about everything, never resting until she knew the price of every part of Marianne's outfit. She could have estimated the total number of her gowns more accurately than Marianne herself. She also hoped, before they parted, to discover the weekly cost of her laundry and her annual allowance for personal expenses. These intrusive investigations generally ended with a compliment intended to soften them, but which Marianne considered the greatest intrusion of all. After an examination of the cost and making of her gown, the colour of her shoes, and the arrangement of her hair, she was almost certain to hear that “upon her word, she looked wonderfully smart, and would surely make a great many conquests.”

With encouragement of this kind, Marianne was sent to her brother's carriage on the present occasion. Both sisters were ready to enter it within five minutes of its arrival. Their punctuality did not please their sister-in-law, who had gone ahead to her acquaintance's house and was hoping they would delay enough to inconvenience either her or her coachman.

Nothing very remarkable happened that evening. Like other musical parties, it contained many people who genuinely appreciated the performance, and many more who did not appreciate it at all. The performers, as usual, were in their own opinion and that of their closest friends the finest amateur musicians in England.

Elinor was not musical and did not pretend to be. She therefore felt no hesitation in looking away from the grand piano whenever she wished. Even the presence of a harp and cello could not restrain her from directing her eyes towards any other object in the room. During one such wandering glance, she noticed among a group of young men the very gentleman who had lectured them on toothpick cases at Gray's. Soon afterwards she saw him looking at her and speaking familiarly with her brother. She had just decided to ask John his name when both men approached, and Mr. Dashwood introduced him as Mr. Robert Ferrars.

He addressed her with easy politeness, twisting his head into a bow that confirmed, as clearly as words could, that he was exactly the conceited fool Lucy had described. How fortunate for Elinor if her love for Edward had depended less on his own worth than on the worth of his closest relations! His brother's bow would then have completed the work begun by his mother's and sister's bad temper. But, though she wondered at the difference between the brothers, she did not find that one's emptiness and vanity destroyed her affection for the other's modesty and goodness. Robert himself explained why they _were_ so different in the course of fifteen minutes' conversation. Speaking of Edward and regretting the extreme social awkwardness which he truly believed kept him out of proper society, Robert candidly and generously attributed it less to any natural defect than to the misfortune of private education. He himself, though probably not born with any particular or substantial superiority, had become as fit for society as any man simply through attending a public school.

“Upon my soul,” he added, “I believe that is the whole explanation. I often tell my mother so when she worries about it. ‘My dear mother,’ I always say, ‘you must stop troubling yourself. Nothing can mend it now, and it is entirely your own doing. Why did you let my uncle Sir Robert persuade you, against your own judgement, to place Edward with a private tutor at the most important stage of his life? If you had sent him to Westminster with me instead of to Mr. Pratt's, none of this would have happened.’ That is how I always see the matter, and my mother is thoroughly convinced of her mistake.”
Elinor did not challenge his opinion. Whatever she thought in general of the advantages of a public school, she could take no satisfaction in Edward's having lived with Mr. Pratt's family.
“You live in Devonshire, I believe,” he next observed, “in a cottage near Dawlish.”

Elinor corrected him about its location. He seemed rather surprised that anyone could live in Devonshire without living near Dawlish. He nevertheless gave his hearty approval to their choice of a cottage.

“For my part,” he said, “I am excessively fond of cottages. They are always so comfortable, so elegant. I declare that, if I had money to spare, I would buy a little land and build one myself not far from London. I could drive down whenever I liked, gather a few friends round me, and be happy. I tell everyone who plans to build to build a cottage. My friend Lord Courtland came expressly to ask my advice the other day and showed me three different designs by Bonomi. I was to choose the best. ‘My dear Courtland,’ I said, immediately throwing all three into the fire, ‘don't use any of them. Whatever you do, build a cottage.’ And I imagine that will settle it.

“Some people think a cottage cannot have any space or conveniences, but they are quite wrong. Last month I visited my friend Elliott near Dartford. Lady Elliott wanted to give a dance. ‘But how can we manage it?’ she asked. ‘My dear Ferrars, do tell me what to do. No room in this cottage will hold ten couples, and where could we serve supper?’ _I_ saw at once that there was no difficulty. ‘My dear Lady Elliott,’ I said, ‘don't trouble yourself. The dining room will easily hold eighteen couples; put the card tables in the drawing room; open the library for tea and other refreshments; and have supper laid out in the saloon.’ She was delighted. We measured the dining room and found that it held exactly eighteen couples. Everything was arranged precisely according to my plan. So you see, provided people know how to go about it, a cottage can offer every comfort just as well as the largest house.”
Elinor agreed with everything. She did not consider him worth the compliment of a reasoned disagreement.

John Dashwood enjoyed music no more than his eldest sister, so his mind was equally free to occupy itself elsewhere. During the evening an idea occurred to him which he put to his wife for approval when they returned home. Mrs. Dennison's mistaken assumption that his sisters were their guests had suggested that it might be proper to invite them to become so while Mrs. Jennings was kept away from home. It would cost nothing and cause no more inconvenience. Altogether, it was an attention which his sensitive conscience considered necessary to release him completely from his promise to his father. Fanny was startled by the proposal.

“I don't see how we could do it without offending Lady Middleton,” she said. “They spend every day with her. Otherwise I would be delighted. You know I am always ready to show them any kindness in my power, as taking them out tonight proves. But they are Lady Middleton's guests. How can I ask them away from her?”

Very humbly, her husband failed to understand the force of this objection. They had already spent a week of days in Conduit Street; Lady Middleton surely could not object to their giving the same number to such close relations.
Fanny paused briefly, then spoke again with renewed energy.

“My dear, I would invite them with all my heart if I could. But I had just decided to ask the Miss Steeles to stay with us for a few days. They are very well-behaved, good sort of girls, and I think we owe them the attention, since their uncle did so well by Edward. We can invite your sisters another year. The Miss Steeles may never come to London again. I am sure you will like them. Indeed, you _do_ like them very much already, you know, and so does my mother. And Harry is so fond of them!”

Mr. Dashwood was convinced. He saw the need to invite the Miss Steeles immediately. Resolving to invite his sisters another year soothed his conscience, though he privately suspected that another year would remove the need for any invitation: Elinor would come to London as Colonel Brandon's wife, and Marianne as _their_ guest.

Delighted at her escape and proud of the quick thinking that had secured it, Fanny wrote to Lucy the next morning. She invited her and her sister to spend several days in Harley Street as soon as Lady Middleton could spare them. This gave Lucy real and reasonable cause for happiness. Mrs. Dashwood seemed actually to be working on her behalf, encouraging every hope and advancing every plan. Nothing could matter more to her interests than such an opportunity to be with Edward and his family; nothing could flatter her feelings more than this invitation. No gratitude could be too great, and no acceptance too prompt. Their visit to Lady Middleton, whose duration had previously been unfixed, was immediately discovered to have been intended all along to end in two days.

The note was shown to Elinor within ten minutes of its arrival. For the first time it led her to share some of Lucy's hopes. Such unusual kindness, offered after so short an acquaintance, seemed to show that their goodwill towards Lucy arose from more than mere spite against Elinor. With time and skilful management, it might achieve everything Lucy wanted. Her flattery had already overcome Lady Middleton's pride and gained entry into Mrs. John Dashwood's closed heart. Such results opened the possibility of still greater ones.

The Miss Steeles moved to Harley Street. Everything Elinor heard about their influence there strengthened her expectation of the outcome. Sir John called more than once and brought back accounts of their favour which must have impressed anyone. Mrs. Dashwood had never liked any young women so much in her life. She had given each a needle case made by an emigrant, called Lucy by her first name, and did not know whether she could ever bear to part with them.

chapters.title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: By the end of a fortnight, Mrs. Palmer was so well that her mother no longer felt obliged to devote all her time to her. Content now to visit once or twice a day, she returned to her own home and habits. The Miss Dashwoods were very willing to resume their former share in that routine.

On about the third or fourth morning after they had settled back into Berkeley Street, Mrs. Jennings returned from her usual visit to Mrs. Palmer and entered the drawing room, where Elinor was alone. Her air of hurried importance prepared Elinor for something extraordinary. She had barely time to form the thought before Mrs. Jennings confirmed it.
“Lord, my dear Miss Dashwood! Have you heard what has happened?”
“No, ma'am. What is the news?”

“Something so extraordinary! But you shall hear everything. When I arrived at Mr. Palmer's, Charlotte was in a terrible fuss about the baby. She was certain he was very ill: he cried and fretted and was covered in spots. I looked at him immediately. ‘Lord, my dear,’ I said, ‘it is only the red gum, an ordinary infant's rash.’ The nurse said exactly the same. But Charlotte would not be satisfied, so we sent for Mr. Donavan. Fortunately, he had just returned from Harley Street and could come straight over. The moment he saw the baby, he said just what we had: nothing but the red gum. Then Charlotte was satisfied. As he was about to leave, it occurred to me—I really cannot think what put it into my head—to ask whether there was any news. At that he smiled and smirked, then looked serious, and seemed to know something. At last he whispered, ‘In case any worrying report about their sister-in-law's illness reaches the young ladies staying with you, I think I ought to say that there is no great cause for alarm. I hope Mrs. Dashwood will recover very well.’”
“What! Is Fanny unwell?”

“That is exactly what I said, my dear. ‘Lord,’ I said, ‘is Mrs. Dashwood ill?’ Then the whole story came out. From everything I can gather, this is the long and short of it. Mr. Edward Ferrars—the very young man I used to tease you about, though I am enormously glad now that there was never anything in it—Mr. Edward Ferrars has apparently been engaged to my cousin Lucy for more than a year! What do you think of that, my dear? And nobody knew a word except Nancy! Could you have believed it possible? It is no great wonder that they should like each other, but that things should have gone so far without anyone suspecting—that _is_ strange. I never happened to see them together, or I am sure I should have discovered it immediately. Well, they kept it all a great secret for fear of Mrs. Ferrars. Neither she nor your brother or his wife suspected a thing until this very morning, when poor Nancy, who is well-meaning but no genius, blurted it all out. ‘Lord,’ she must have thought, ‘they are all so fond of Lucy, surely they won't object.’ Off she went to your sister-in-law, who was sitting alone at her carpet-work, little imagining what was coming. Only five minutes earlier she had been telling your brother she meant to arrange a marriage between Edward and some lord's daughter—I forget whose. You can imagine the blow to all her pride and vanity. She immediately went into violent hysterics, screaming so loudly that your brother heard from his dressing room downstairs, where he was considering writing to his steward in the country. He rushed up, and there was a dreadful scene. Lucy had joined them by then, without the least idea of what was happening. Poor creature, I pity _her_. I must say she was treated very harshly. Your sister-in-law raged like a fury and soon made her faint. Nancy went down on her knees, crying bitterly, while your brother walked about saying he did not know what to do. Mrs. Dashwood declared they should not stay in the house another minute. Your brother had to kneel as well to persuade her to let them remain long enough to pack their clothes. _Then_ she had another fit of hysterics, and he was so frightened that he insisted on sending for Mr. Donavan. He found the whole house in an uproar. The carriage was at the door to take my poor cousins away, and they were getting into it as he left. He says poor Lucy could scarcely walk, and Nancy was nearly as bad. I declare I have no patience with your sister-in-law, and I sincerely hope the marriage takes place in spite of her. Lord, how upset poor Mr. Edward will be when he hears! To have his beloved treated with such scorn! They say he is terribly fond of her, as he well may be. I shouldn't wonder if he flies into a furious rage. Mr. Donavan thinks so too. We talked a great deal about it. And the best part is that he has gone back to Harley Street to be close at hand when Mrs. Ferrars hears. They sent for her the moment my cousins left, because your sister-in-law was certain _she_ would have hysterics too. Well, she may, for all I care. I pity neither of them. I cannot stand people making such a fuss over money and rank. There is no reason on earth why Edward and Lucy should not marry. Mrs. Ferrars can certainly afford to provide very handsomely for her son. Lucy may have next to nothing, but nobody knows better how to make the most of everything. If his mother would allow him just five hundred a year, I dare say Lucy could make as good a showing as anyone else on eight hundred. Lord, how comfortably they could live in a cottage like yours, or a little larger, with two maids and two menservants! I believe I could find them a housemaid, too. My Betty has a sister out of work who would suit them perfectly.”

Mrs. Jennings stopped. Elinor had had plenty of time to collect her thoughts and was able to make a reply and offer comments as the subject naturally required. She was glad that nobody suspected her of any special interest in it; glad that Mrs. Jennings had stopped imagining her in love with Edward, as she had lately often hoped; and, above all, glad that Marianne was absent. She felt quite able to discuss the affair without embarrassment and to judge, as she believed impartially, the conduct of everyone involved.

She could scarcely decide what outcome she herself expected. She earnestly tried to banish any notion that it might ultimately end otherwise than in Edward's marriage to Lucy. She wanted to hear what Mrs. Ferrars would say and do, though the nature of her response could not be doubted. Still more, she wanted to know how Edward would behave. For _him_ she felt great compassion. For Lucy she felt very little, and had to work to find even that little. For the rest of the party she felt none at all.

Since Mrs. Jennings could discuss nothing else, Elinor soon realised that Marianne must be prepared to hear it. There was no time to lose in correcting her mistake, telling her the truth, and trying to make her able to hear others discuss it without betraying distress for her sister or resentment towards Edward.

It was a painful duty. Elinor was about to take away what she truly believed was Marianne's chief comfort, reveal facts about Edward that might destroy him for ever in her good opinion, and make her relive her own disappointment through a likeness between their situations which _she_ would find striking. Unwelcome as the task was, however, it had to be done, and Elinor hurried to do it.

She had no desire to dwell on her own feelings or present herself as deeply suffering. The only exception was that the self-control she had practised since learning of Edward's engagement might show Marianne what was possible. Her account was clear and simple. She could not give it without feeling, but there was no violent agitation or passionate grief. _Those_ belonged to her listener: Marianne heard her with horror and wept bitterly. Elinor had to comfort others in her own distress as much as in theirs. She readily offered every reassurance her own calm could supply, and defended Edward earnestly against every charge except lack of judgement.

For some time, Marianne would believe neither the reassurance nor the defence. Edward seemed another Willoughby. Since Elinor admitted that she _had_ loved him deeply, how could she suffer less than Marianne herself? As for Lucy Steele, Marianne considered her so utterly unlovable, so incapable of attracting an intelligent man, that at first she could not believe Edward had ever loved her, and afterwards could not forgive him for it. She would not even admit that it was natural. Elinor left her to be persuaded by the only thing that could persuade her: a better understanding of human nature.

In her first account, Elinor had got no further than the fact of the engagement and how long it had existed. Marianne's feelings had then interrupted, making an orderly explanation impossible. For some time Elinor could only soothe her distress, ease her fears, and resist her indignation. The first question that led to further details was,
“How long have you known this, Elinor? Has Edward written to tell you?”
“I have known for four months. When Lucy first came to Barton Park last November, she told me about the engagement in confidence.”
Marianne's eyes expressed an astonishment her lips could not put into words. After a pause of wonder, she exclaimed,
“Four months! Have you known all this for four months?”
Elinor said she had.
“What! While you were caring for me through all my misery, you had this on your heart? And I reproached you for being happy!”
“It would not have been right for you to know then how far I was from happiness.”
“Four months!” Marianne cried again. “So calm, so cheerful! What has kept you going?”

“The knowledge that I was doing my duty. My promise to Lucy required secrecy. I owed it to her to give no hint of the truth. And I owed it to my family and friends not to make them anxious about me when I could offer no explanation to relieve that anxiety.”
Marianne looked deeply affected.
“I have often wanted to correct your expectations and our mother's,” Elinor added. “Once or twice I even tried. But I could never convince you without betraying the confidence placed in me.”
“Four months! And you still loved him!”

“Yes. But he was not the only person I loved. Because other people's comfort mattered to me, I was glad to spare them the knowledge of how much I felt. Now I can think and talk about it with little agitation. I do not want you to suffer for me, because I assure you I no longer suffer greatly myself. Many things sustain me. I know of no foolishness of my own that brought this disappointment about. I have borne it as far as possible without making others share it. I do not believe Edward guilty of any fundamental wrongdoing. I wish him every happiness, and I am so certain he will always do his duty that, whatever regrets he may have now, he must become happy in the end. Lucy is not without intelligence, and that is a foundation on which every good quality may be built. After all, Marianne, however enchanting the idea of one unchanging love, and whatever we may say about our happiness depending entirely on one particular person, it is not intended—it is not right—it is not possible that this should be so. Edward will marry Lucy. He will marry a woman more attractive and more intelligent than half her sex. Time and habit will teach him to forget that he ever thought another woman superior to _her_.”

“If that is how you think,” Marianne said, “if losing what you value most can be so easily compensated for by something else, perhaps your determination and self-control are a little less astonishing. I can understand them rather better.”

“I understand you. You don't believe I have ever felt very much. For four months, Marianne, all this has weighed on my mind without my being free to speak of it to a single person. I knew it would make you and our mother deeply unhappy whenever you learnt it, yet I could do nothing to prepare you. It was told to me—almost forced on me—by the very woman whose earlier engagement destroyed all my hopes. And she told me, I thought, triumphantly. I have had to counter her suspicions by trying to seem indifferent where I cared most deeply. Not just once: again and again I have had to listen to her hopes and her triumph. I have known I was separated from Edward for ever without hearing a single fact that could make me want him less. Nothing has shown him unworthy, and nothing has shown that he is indifferent to me. I have had to bear his sister's unkindness and his mother's insolence, suffering the penalties of an attachment without enjoying its advantages. All this has happened at a time when, as you know only too well, it has not been my only unhappiness. If you can believe me capable of feeling anything at all, surely you can believe I have suffered _now_. The calm with which I can at last consider it, the comfort I have allowed myself to accept, are the results of constant, painful effort. They did not appear by themselves. They did not come to relieve me at the beginning. No, Marianne. _Then_, if I had not been bound to silence, perhaps nothing—not even what I owed my dearest friends—could have entirely prevented me from showing openly that I was _very_ unhappy.”
Marianne was completely humbled.

“Oh, Elinor!” she cried. “You have made me hate myself for ever. How cruel I have been to you! You have been my only comfort, endured me through all my misery, seemed to suffer only for me. Is this my gratitude? Is this all I can give you in return? Because your goodness condemns me, I have tried to deny it.”

The confession was followed by the most affectionate embraces. In Marianne's present state of mind, Elinor had no difficulty in obtaining any promise she asked. At her request, Marianne undertook never to discuss the affair with anyone in the slightest tone of bitterness; to meet Lucy without revealing any increase in dislike; and even, if chance brought them together, to see Edward with all her usual warmth. These were great concessions. But when Marianne felt she had wronged someone, no effort to make amends could be too great.

She kept her promise of discretion admirably. She listened to everything Mrs. Jennings said without changing colour, disagreed with nothing, and was heard three times to say, “Yes, ma'am.” She heard Lucy praised with no response beyond moving from one chair to another. When Mrs. Jennings spoke of Edward's love, it cost her only a tightening in the throat. Such progress towards heroism in her sister made Elinor feel capable of anything herself.
The next morning brought a further test. Their brother arrived, wearing an expression of the utmost seriousness, to discuss the dreadful affair and report on his wife's condition.
“I suppose you have heard,” he said with great solemnity as soon as he sat down, “of the shocking discovery made under our roof yesterday.”
Their expressions showed that they had. The moment seemed too terrible for anyone to speak.

“Your sister-in-law has suffered dreadfully,” he continued. “Mrs. Ferrars too. In short, there has been such a complicated scene of distress—but I hope we may weather the storm without any of us being entirely overcome. Poor Fanny! She was in hysterics all day yesterday. Still, I must not alarm you too much. Donavan says there is no serious cause for concern. She has a strong constitution and resolution equal to anything. She has borne it all with the courage of an angel. She says she will never think well of anyone again. Who could wonder, after such deception, such ingratitude, where so much kindness and trust had been shown? She invited these young women entirely out of the goodness of her heart, simply because she thought they deserved attention, were harmless, well-behaved girls, and would make pleasant company. Otherwise we had both very much wanted to invite you and Marianne while your kind friend here was caring for her daughter. And now this is the reward! ‘I wish with all my heart,’ poor Fanny says in her affectionate way, ‘that we had invited your sisters instead.’”
He stopped here to receive their thanks. Once they had supplied them, he continued.

“It is impossible to describe what poor Mrs. Ferrars suffered when Fanny first told her. While she had been lovingly planning such an excellent marriage for him, who could have imagined he was secretly engaged to someone else all along? Such a suspicion could never have entered her head. If she suspected _any_ attachment elsewhere, it could not have been _there_. ‘Surely,’ she said, ‘I might have thought myself safe in _that_ quarter.’ She was in absolute anguish. We discussed what to do, and finally she decided to send for Edward. He came, but I am sorry to tell you what followed. Everything his mother said to make him end the engagement was useless, even with the help, as you can imagine, of my arguments and Fanny's pleas. Duty, affection, everything was ignored. I never imagined Edward could be so stubborn and unfeeling. His mother explained her generous plans if he married Miss Morton. She would settle the Norfolk estate on him, bringing in a full thousand a year after land tax. When matters grew desperate, she even offered to make it twelve hundred. On the other hand, if he persisted in this low connection, she showed him the poverty that must follow. His own two thousand pounds would be all he ever had, she declared. She would never see him again. Far from giving him the smallest help, if he entered any profession to support himself better, she would do everything she could to prevent his advancement.”
At this Marianne struck her hands together in a burst of indignation. “Good heavens!” she cried. “Can such a thing be possible?”
“You may well be astonished, Marianne,” her brother replied, “at the stubbornness that could resist arguments like these. Your exclamation is perfectly natural.”
Marianne was about to answer sharply, but remembered her promises and held back.

“Yet all this was urged in vain,” he continued. “Edward said little, but what he did say was absolutely firm. Nothing would persuade him to abandon his engagement. He would keep it, whatever it cost him.”

“Then he behaved like an honest man!” Mrs. Jennings cried with blunt sincerity, unable to remain silent. “Forgive me, Mr. Dashwood, but I would have thought him a scoundrel if he had done anything else. I have some interest in the matter too. Lucy Steele is my cousin, and I believe no better sort of girl exists, nor one more deserving of a good husband.”
John Dashwood was greatly astonished. But he had a calm nature, was not easily provoked, and never wanted to offend anyone, especially anyone wealthy. He therefore replied without resentment.

“I would never wish to speak disrespectfully of a relation of yours, ma'am. Miss Lucy Steele is no doubt a very deserving young woman. But in this case, you understand, the connection must be impossible. Entering a secret engagement with a young man in her uncle's care, the son, moreover, of a woman as wealthy as Mrs. Ferrars, is perhaps a little extraordinary altogether. In short, Mrs. Jennings, I have no wish to criticise the behaviour of anyone you value. We all wish her every happiness. Mrs. Ferrars, throughout, has behaved as any conscientious, good mother would in the same circumstances. She has shown dignity and generosity. Edward has chosen his own fate, and I fear it will be an unhappy one.”
Marianne sighed out the same fear. Elinor's heart ached for Edward, facing his mother's threats for a woman who could never reward his sacrifice.
“Well, sir,” Mrs. Jennings asked, “and how did it all end?”

“I am sorry to say, ma'am, in a most unhappy separation. Edward has been cast out of his mother's favour for ever. He left her house yesterday. Where he went, or whether he remains in London, I do not know. Naturally, _we_ cannot inquire.”
“Poor young man! What will become of him now?”

“What indeed, ma'am? It is a melancholy thought. Born with the prospect of such wealth! I cannot imagine a more deplorable situation. How can a man live on the interest from two thousand pounds? And remember that, but for his own foolishness, within three months he might have had two thousand five hundred a year, since Miss Morton has thirty thousand pounds. I cannot picture greater wretchedness. We must all feel for him, especially since it is entirely beyond our power to help.”

“Poor young man!” Mrs. Jennings cried. “He would certainly be welcome to a room and meals in my house. I would tell him so if I could see him. He ought not to be paying to live in lodgings and taverns now.”
Elinor thanked her inwardly for this kindness to Edward, though she could not help smiling at the form it took.

“If only he had treated himself as well as his friends wished to treat him,” John Dashwood said, “he could now be in his proper position and lack nothing. As it is, nobody can possibly help him. And something further is being prepared against him, worse than everything else. With a very natural spirit, his mother has decided to settle immediately on Robert _the very estate_ Edward might have had on the proper conditions. I left her discussing it with her lawyer this morning.”
“Well,” Mrs. Jennings said, “that is _her_ revenge. Everyone has their own way. But mine would hardly be to make one son independent of me because the other had annoyed me.”
Marianne rose and began walking about the room.
“What could wound a man's pride more,” John continued, “than to see his younger brother owning an estate that might have been his? Poor Edward! I sincerely feel for him.”

A few more minutes of similar expressions ended his visit. Repeatedly assuring his sisters that he believed Fanny's illness posed no serious danger, and that they therefore need not be very anxious, he finally took his leave and departed. He left the three ladies entirely agreed, at least in their opinions of Mrs. Ferrars's conduct, the Dashwoods', and Edward's.

The moment he left the room, Marianne's indignation burst out. Her vehemence made restraint impossible for Elinor and unnecessary for Mrs. Jennings, and all three joined in a spirited criticism of those involved.

chapters.title: Chapter 38
paragraphs: Mrs. Jennings praised Edward's behaviour warmly, but only Elinor and Marianne understood its true worth.
